8                     UNITED STATES DISTRICT COURT                           
9                   SOUTHERN DISTRICT OF CALIFORNIA                          
10                                                                            
11  KIMERA LABS INC,                     Case No.:  21-cv-2137-MMA-DDL        

12                             Plaintiff,                                     
                                        ORDER FOLLOWING MOTION               
13  v.                                   HEARING ON MAY 8, 2024               

14  EXOCEL BIO INC., et al.,                                                  
                                        [Dkt. Nos. 233, 235]                 
15                          Defendants.                                       
16                                                                            
17       On May 8, 2024, the Court heard oral argument on multiple discovery-related 
18  motions.  Having considered the parties’ briefing and the arguments of counsel, the Court 
19  GRANTS   Defendants’  motion  to  compel  deposition  testimony  [Dkt.  No.  233]  and 
20  DENIES Plaintiffs’ motions for leave to serve third party subpoenas and to compel 
21  production of financial information [Dkt. No. 235] as set forth below:    
22                       Plaintiff’s Motions (Dkt. No. 235)                   
23  Motion for Leave to Serve Third Party Subpoenas                           
24       For the reasons stated on the record at the May 8 hearing, the Court DENIES 
25  Plaintiff’s motion to for leave to serve additional third party subpoenas.  Plaintiff’s counsel 
26  clarified at the motion hearing that Plaintiff seeks to issue seven third party subpoenas; 
27  however, the motion does not describe why Plaintiff believes each of these third parties 
28                                                                            
1  have information that is relevant to a claim or defense or what specific information Plaintiff 
2  would seek through the subpoenas.                                         
3       Plaintiff’s  counsel  clarified  at  the  hearing  that  the  proposed  subpoenas  seek 
4  documents exchanged between Defendants and the third parties, but Plaintiff has  not 
5  sought leave to propound additional requests for production on Exocel Bio.  See Fed. R. 
6  Civ. P. 26(b)(2)(C)(i) (court must limit the extent of discovery otherwise allowed if “the 
7  discovery sought is unreasonably cumulative or duplicative, or can be obtained from some 
8  other source that is more convenient, less burdensome, or less expensive”);  Nidec Corp. 
9  v. Victor Co. of Japan, 249 F.R.D. 575, 577 (N.D. Cal. 2007) (“There is simply no reason 
10  to  burden  nonparties  when  the  documents  sought  are  in  possession  of  the  party 
11  defendant.”);  Amini Innovation Corp. v. McFerran Home Furnishings, Inc., 300 F.R.D. 
12  406, 410 (C.D. Cal. 2014) (“A court may prohibit a party from obtaining discovery from a 
13  non-party if that same information is available from another party to the litigation.”) 
14  (citation omitted).                                                       
15       As discussed at the hearing, the Court will allow each side to propound up to ten 
16  requests for production (“RFPs”) as follows:                              
17       Both sides must serve their RFPs by not later than May 13, 2024.     
18       The parties must meet and confer regarding the RFPs by not later than May 15, 
19  2024.                                                                     
20       If there are any outstanding objections to any RFPs following the meet and confer, 
21  the parties must file a joint motion for determination of discovery dispute by not later than 
22  May 20, 2024.  The joint motion shall consist of a chart containing the text of the disputed 
23  discovery response and each party’s position (in one or two sentences) regarding the RFP. 
24       The Court will hold a motion hearing to resolve any disputes on May 29, 2024, at 
25  8:30 a.m. via Zoom.                                                       
26  Motion to Compel Production of Financial Documents                        
27       For the reasons stated at the May 8 hearing, the Court DENIES Plaintiff’s motion 
28  to compel production of financial documents.  Defendants have produced Exocel Bio’s 
1  general ledger for 2021 and 2022, and they will produce the 2023 general ledger promptly 
2  when it is finalized on or before September 1, 2024.  Exocel Bio will prepare an exhibit for 
3  its Rule 30(b)(6) deposition that contains the attorney’s fees expenses reflected in the 
4  general ledger and a separate figure showing the fees incurred by Exocel Bio in defending 
5  this litigation.  The Court DENIES Plaintiff’s request to require Exocel Bio to provide 
6  redacted attorney invoices for this litigation.                           
7         Defendants’ Motion to Compel Deposition Testimony (Dkt. No. 233)   
8       For the reasons stated on the record at the May 8 hearing, the Court GRANTS 
9  Defendants’  motion  to  compel  deposition  testimony.    At  the  deposition  of  Maryel 
10  Gonzalez-Perez, Plaintiff’s Chief Regulatory Officer, Plaintiff’s counsel instructed the 
11  deponent not to answer multiple questions on the grounds of “trade secret privilege.”  
12  “Questions of privilege that arise in the course of the adjudication of federal rights are 
13  governed by the principles of the common law as they may be interpreted by the courts of 
14  the United States in the light of reason and experience.”  United States v. Zolin, 491 U.S. 
15  554, 562 (1989) (citing Fed. R. Evid. 501).  Federal privilege law applies here because 
16  Plaintiff asserts violations of the federal Defend Trade Secrets Act, 18 U.S.C. § 1836, et 
17  seq.                                                                      
18       Plaintiff’s  authorities  do  not  support  the  existence  of  a  federal  “trade  secret 
19  privilege” per se.  See Terry v. Register Tapes Unlimited, Inc., 2:16-CV-0806-WBSAC, 
20  2017 WL 3226867, at *3 (E.D. Cal. July 31, 2017) (applying California state law trade 
21  secret privilege).   Rather, the issue is whether  defense counsel’s questions regarding 
22  changes to Kimera Labs’ exosome manufacturing processes from 2019 to the present seek 
23  information that is relevant to a claim or defense and proportional to the needs of the case 
24  under Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b).  The Court concludes that questions regarding changes in the 
25  “Kimera Process” seek information that is relevant to the existence of a trade secret, the 
26  value of the trade secret, and the appropriate scope of injunctive relief if Plaintiff were to 
27  prevail  on  its  trade  secret  misappropriation  claim.    The  information  sought  is  also 
28                                                                            
1 || proportional to the needs of the case and can be gathered through Ms. Gonzalez-Perez’s 
2 || deposition. 
3         The Court is mindful of Plaintiff's concerns with providing additional information 
4   ||regarding its trade secrets; however, the parties agreed that Plaintiff may designate  such 
5   ||testimony  as  “CONFIDENTIAL-FOR  COUNSEL  ONLY”  under  the  protective  order. 
6 || Dkt. No.  124. 
7         IT IS SO ORDERED. 
8   ||Dated:  May 9, 2024                      _—
